messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo had always lived in his body. For sixty-two years, it was his instrument, his voice, his home. As a dancer and choreographer, he commanded it with a grace that defied his age. But four months ago, on his way to a dress rehearsal, that home was violated. A truck ran a red light, and the world dissolved into the deafening shriek of tires and the percussive, final crunch of metal. He remembers the sound more than anything, a visceral auditory scar that has refused to fade. The details remain a blur, a chaotic sequence he has never been able to arrange into a story. When he tries, the words fail him, as if the memory exists only in sensation, not language.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo tried to force a return to normalcy, but his body, once a source of pride, had become a source of terror. The world felt peppered with ambushes. A car backfiring on the street would send a jolt of horror through him, instantly conjuring the sound of the crash. This raw, physical sense of threat would drag the memory back with it, not as a cohesive narrative, but as a sensory fragment—always that terrible sound, accompanied by a wave of shame so profound it felt like a physical sickness. He felt ashamed of his helplessness, pinned in the driver's seat, a passive victim. The shame was the worst part, and it was this feeling, more than the fear itself, that drove him to desperate measures. He began trying to push the thoughts away, a constant, exhausting effort to police the borders of his own mind. At night, he would stay up until three or four in the morning, watching old movies until he was too tired to dream, terrified of what awaited him in the dark.

These strategies became a damaging ritual. His attempts to suppress the memory only seemed to give it more power; the auditory fragments would erupt without warning, louder and more startling than before. When the memories did break through, he would deliberately try to leave his body, to blank out and feel nothing, staring at a wall in his studio until the world went fuzzy. This deliberate dissociation, meant to be an escape, only fractured the memory further, making it feel even more alien and unspeakable. The failure of these efforts fed a growing belief that he was fundamentally broken. Staying up all night left him frayed and jumpy, which he interpreted not as exhaustion, but as proof of his flawed character. He had come to believe the accident happened because of who he is—too proud, too focused, someone deserving of punishment.

This deep-seated conviction that he is both helpless and inherently flawed now governs his entire existence, making him see danger everywhere. The belief that he is powerless to stop bad things from happening has transformed his dance studio, once a sanctuary, into a space of constant threat-monitoring. He finds himself unable to focus on his students, instead scanning the exits as soon as he enters, plotting escape routes from a room he has known for twenty years. His body is coiled with a tension that makes his art impossible. When a young dancer recently touched his arm to ask a question, he flinched so violently the student recoiled in alarm. This constant state of high alert, the potent cocktail of fear and shame that simmers just below his skin, serves as daily confirmation of his darkest appraisals. The fear is no longer just a reaction; it is evidence that he will never feel normal emotions again, that the joy he once found in music and movement is lost to him forever.

The man who could once lose himself in a performance is now a prisoner of his own vigilance. His wife, Elena, watches him with a growing sense of alarm, seeing a man who is physically present but emotionally absent. It was after he found he could no longer listen to the music for a new piece—the swelling strings sounding not like passion but like a prelude to disaster—that he finally sought help. He confessed to Elena that he felt like a ghost haunting his own life. Mateo now sits in the waiting room, terrified that his belief is true: that he is permanently changed, and that the man he was died in the wreckage four months ago.
